examples.title: The friendly IT call that wasn't — Aflac

story30.howItWorked: A calm, credible caller guided an employee into approving an MFA prompt the employee didn’t initiate.
whatToNotice: Unsolicited IT call with no ticket or known issue
Pressure to approve an authentication prompt
Caller knew personal/work details (often scraped from LinkedIn)
whatToDo: Hang up and call IT back using a known number
Never approve MFA prompts you didn’t initiate

checkIn.question: You receive an unexpected call from “IT” asking you to approve an MFA prompt. What should you do?

choices.label: Approve it quickly so you don’t get locked out
Hang up and call IT back using the official directory number
Share your username so they can look you up

checkIn.explanation: Unsolicited IT calls can be vishing. Never approve MFA prompts you didn’t initiate—verify using a known channel.

examples.scenario:
It started like any ordinary morning. Employees were logging in, checking emails, grabbing coffee. Then someone's phone rang.

"Hi, this is Daniel from Tech Support. We're running a quick credential sync due to a recent security update. Nothing to worry about — I'll walk you through it. Can you just confirm your username?"

The voice was calm, professional, and friendly. The caller knew the employee's name, department, and manager. There was no reason to doubt them.

"Now you'll get a prompt on your phone. Just hit approve — it's a one-time thing."

And just like that — the door was open.

The attackers were a group known as Scattered Spider. They don't rely on viruses or code. They use something far more powerful: people. From that single phone call, they gained access to internal systems containing insurance claims, employee records, and Social Security numbers.
redFlags: IT never calls out of the blue to ask for your credentials — real helpdesk calls follow a ticket or known issue
"Just approve this pop-up" — if you didn't initiate the login, never approve an authentication prompt
Urgency language: "you'll get locked out if you don't act now"
Caller knows your name and department — this information is often public on LinkedIn
examples.whyItWasPhishing: This is vishing — voice phishing. The attackers researched the company structure to sound credible, then used psychological pressure to rush the employee into approving a real Microsoft Authenticator prompt. That approval handed over live account access instantly.
examples.whatToDo: Hang up. Never share credentials or approve authentication prompts you didn't initiate. Call your real IT helpdesk back using a number from your company's official directory. Report the attempt even if you didn't fall for it — it helps IT warn others.

examples.title: One fake Apple email brought down Sony Pictures
examples.meta: Credential phishing · Spear phishing · Corporate data breach

story30.attackGoal: Steal credentials to access the corporate network.
story30.howItWorked: A convincing Apple-style alert drove a busy executive to sign in via a link to a fake login page.
whatToNotice: Unexpected security alert urging immediate action
Login page reached via email link (not typed directly)
Credentials requested before you can see any account details
whatToDo: Open a new tab and navigate to the service yourself
Enable MFA so a stolen password isn’t enough

checkIn.question: You get a security alert email claiming your account is locked and you must sign in. What’s the safest first step?

choices.label: Click the link and sign in to check what happened
Open a new tab and go to the official site/app directly
Reply to the email asking for confirmation

checkIn.explanation: Don’t sign in via email links. Navigate directly to the official site/app so you control where you’re logging in.

examples.scenario:
It started with a fake Apple ID alert — the kind most people have seen at least once. "Your account has been locked. Suspicious login detected. Click here to verify your device."

A Sony executive received exactly that email in late 2014. It looked like Apple. It linked to what appeared to be a real Apple login page. Distracted and multitasking, the executive clicked and entered their credentials.

That single action opened the floodgates.

Within days, attackers had access to Sony's internal network. They quietly moved through systems, exfiltrated files, and downloaded confidential material. When the attack went public, the scope was extraordinary: over 100 terabytes of data stolen, thousands of private executive emails leaked, employee Social Security numbers and salaries exposed, unreleased films published online, and entire systems wiped — screens replaced with a message reading "Hacked by #GOP. This is just the beginning."

Sony Pictures was digitally crippled. The entry point? A phishing email that took seconds to click.
redFlags: Unexpected security alerts from Apple, Microsoft, or Google — go directly to their site instead of clicking
"Immediate action required" — urgency designed to override your instinct to pause
A login page you arrived at via a link rather than by navigating directly yourself
The request asks for credentials before you can see any account information
examples.whyItWasPhishing: The email impersonated Apple's security notifications — a format most people trust on sight. The linked page was a convincing replica designed solely to harvest login credentials. Once entered, attackers used those credentials to pivot into Sony's broader corporate network.
examples.whatToDo: Never enter credentials on a page you arrived at via an email link. If you get a security alert from any service, open a new browser tab and type the address yourself. Enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible — it adds a second lock even if your password is compromised.

examples.title: Google and Facebook paid $100 million to a scammer
examples.meta: Invoice fraud · Business Email Compromise · Vendor impersonation

story30.attackGoal: Get a legitimate company to wire money to attacker accounts.
story30.howItWorked: A scammer impersonated a real vendor with lookalike emails and routine-looking invoices.
whatToNotice: Payment changes communicated only via email
A domain that looks almost right
whatToDo: Verify payment changes by calling a known vendor number
Use two-person review for significant payments

checkIn.question: A vendor emails new bank details for future invoices. What should happen before any payment is made?

choices.label: Update details immediately if the invoice format looks correct
Verify via a separate channel using a known vendor phone number
Ask for the change in writing again to be safe

checkIn.explanation: BEC works by making email look routine. Always verify payment detail changes using a separate trusted channel.

examples.scenario:
Between 2013 and 2015, a scammer named Evaldas Rimasauskas defrauded Google and Facebook out of over $100 million combined — not through hacking, but through fake invoices.

He knew both companies had large contracts with a real company called Quanta Computer, a hardware supplier based in Taiwan. So he registered a company with the same name in Latvia, created email addresses impersonating Quanta employees, and designed invoices that exactly matched the format and style of Quanta's real ones.

Then he sent those invoices to the finance departments at both companies.

The invoices matched the types of payments they made regularly. They looked routine. And so the money was wired — again and again — directly into overseas accounts.

By the time anyone caught on, over $100 million had gone. Rimasauskas was eventually arrested and agreed to repay $49.7 million. The rest was gone.

This wasn't a hack. It was a well-crafted fake invoice sent to the right person at the right time. And it worked on two of the biggest tech companies on Earth.
redFlags: Payment detail changes or new bank account information communicated only through email
Invoices that look identical to ones you normally receive — but from a slightly different domain
No secondary verification through a separate channel before processing payment
Urgency around payment timing: "our old account is closing, please update immediately"
examples.whyItWasPhishing: This is Business Email Compromise (BEC) combined with vendor impersonation. The attacker didn't need to break into any systems — he just needed convincing paperwork and a target that processed payments without independent verification. Trust and routine were the vulnerabilities.
examples.whatToDo: Any change to a vendor's payment details must be verified by calling the vendor directly using a phone number from your existing records — never from the email. Apply a two-person review for significant payments. If it feels routine, that's exactly when to slow down and check.

examples.title: 57 clicks nearly compromised a nuclear research lab — Oak Ridge

story30.attackGoal: Install malware and gain a foothold inside the network.
story30.howItWorked: Routine-looking emails lured clicks; a malicious page silently installed malware via a browser exploit.
whatToNotice: Risk exists even without typing credentials

checkIn.question: Why can a phishing email be dangerous even if it never asks you to type a password?

choices.label: Because malicious pages can exploit vulnerabilities and install malware
Because it makes your inbox slower
Because clicking a link always deletes your files immediately

checkIn.explanation: Some phishing links deliver malware automatically when a page loads (drive‑by attacks). Treat unexpected links as high risk.

examples.scenario:
In 2011, the Oak Ridge National Laboratory — a U.S. Department of Energy facility responsible for nuclear research and national security — was targeted by a phishing campaign.

The attackers sent emails to 530 employees with subject lines like "Policy Update: Action Required" and "Benefits Adjustment Notice." Each email contained a link. The link didn't ask for a password. It simply exploited a vulnerability in Internet Explorer to silently install malware the moment the page loaded.

Only 57 people clicked. Only 2 machines were infected.

But that was enough.

From those two machines, attackers gained a foothold inside the lab's internal network. They began scanning, moving laterally, and attempting to exfiltrate sensitive research data and emails. To contain the threat, Oak Ridge took the extraordinary step of disconnecting its entire network from the internet — effectively pulling the plug on supercomputers mid-operation.

This was a facility staffed by physicists, engineers, and cybersecurity professionals. The attack worked not because of weak technology, but because clicking links out of habit is human nature.
redFlags: HR or policy-style emails with links — especially ones referencing benefits, payroll, or compliance
You don't need to enter anything for damage to occur — just visiting a malicious page can be enough
Generic subject lines designed to seem routine and time-sensitive
Emails arriving during busy periods when people are most likely to click without thinking
examples.whyItWasPhishing: The emails were crafted to blend into the normal rhythm of workplace communications. The payload was silent — no login page, no obvious sign anything was wrong. The malware installed itself in the background the moment the page loaded.
examples.whatToDo: Treat all unexpected links with the same caution as unexpected attachments. Even if an email looks internal and routine, hover over links to check the destination before clicking. When in doubt, report it — even at a nuclear research lab staffed by experts, two clicks was all it took.

examples.title: A typo changed history — the Podesta email hack
examples.meta: Credential phishing · Spear phishing · High-value target

story30.attackGoal: Steal credentials for a high-value email account.
story30.howItWorked: A realistic Google-style alert + urgency pushed a click; a single verification typo removed the last safeguard.
whatToNotice: Lookalike domains and subtle sender differences
whatToDo: Check the exact domain, not the display name
Navigate directly instead of logging in from an email link

checkIn.question: You’re unsure whether a security alert email is legitimate. What’s the safest action?

choices.label: Click the login button and change your password quickly
Forward it to a colleague to decide
Open a new tab and go to the service directly (or contact IT via a known channel)

checkIn.explanation: Don’t authenticate via email links. Navigate directly or verify through a trusted internal channel first.

examples.scenario:
In March 2016, John Podesta — campaign chairman for Hillary Clinton — received an urgent email that appeared to be from Google:

"Someone has your password. We've prevented a sign-in attempt from Ukraine. Click the button below to secure your account."

The email looked real. It sounded urgent. Podesta's team forwarded it to their IT staff to check.

A staffer replied: "This is a legitimate email. John needs to change his password immediately."

They meant to write illegitimate. One word. One typo. Everything changed.

Podesta clicked. The link took him to a spoofed Google login page where he entered his real credentials. Hackers immediately accessed his Gmail account and downloaded over 50,000 emails.

Weeks later, those emails were released by WikiLeaks at the peak of the 2016 US election. The damage was deeply personal, politically explosive, and strategically timed. All of it started with a fake security warning — and a single word typed wrong.
redFlags: The sender domain was googlemail.com — not google.com. One letter of difference.
Security alert emails asking you to click a link and log in — go directly to the site instead
Urgency combined with fear: "someone has your password, act now"
Even people in high-pressure, time-sensitive roles can be caught — urgency is a universal vulnerability
examples.whyItWasPhishing: The email used Google's exact branding, format, and language. The spoofed domain was close enough that most people wouldn't notice the difference. The high-pressure framing — "someone has your password" — was designed to make the recipient act before pausing to verify.
examples.whatToDo: Always check the exact email domain — not just the name displayed. Never click login links from security alert emails; open a new tab and go directly to the service yourself. Enable multi-factor authentication: even if credentials are stolen, MFA means the attacker still can't get in without a second factor you control.
